sections.heading: What is the Binary Search Pattern?
sections.content: Binary Search finds a target in a sorted (or partially ordered) space by repeatedly cutting the search range in half. At each step you compare the middle element with what you want and discard the half that cannot contain the answer. This reduces O(n) to O(log n). The idea goes beyond plain arrays: any time the data has a monotonic property (a yes/no condition that flips only once), you can binary search it.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: The array is sorted (ascending or descending)
The array is rotated or has a peak (bitonic, mountain)
You need the first or last position of a value
You need the insert position, floor or ceiling of a value
The input is huge and O(n) is too slow, so you need O(log n)
Keywords: sorted, rotated, find first, find last, peak, minimum in rotated array, search insert position

Which Loop Condition to Choose
sections.content: Use left <= right when you search for an exact value and return immediately on a match. Use left < right when you search for a boundary: keep mid inside the range when it might be the answer (right = mid) and shrink only when mid is definitely wrong (left = mid + 1). Mixing the styles is the number one source of infinite loops and off-by-one bugs.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Computing mid as (left + right) / 2, which can overflow; use left + (right - left) / 2
Mixing left <= right with right = mid, which creates an infinite loop
Using left = mid when mid is rounded down in a boundary search, which also loops forever
Off by one in the initial right: size for boundary searches, size - 1 for exact matches
Forgetting to check bounds before reading nums[result] after a lower bound search
Comparing with nums[left] instead of nums[right] when finding the rotated minimum
Overflow in mid * mid; convert to Long first
Using binary search on data that is not sorted or monotonic

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Binary search halves the range each step, giving O(log n)
Use left <= right for exact matches and left < right for boundaries
Always compute mid as left + (right - left) / 2
Lower bound is the first index with value >= target, and the pattern gives first and last positions
In a rotated array, one half is always sorted, so decide using that half
Anything with a false...false true...true shape can be binary searched
